title: Hands-on Lab: Does Anger Sound Different from Calm?
text:
The data
We use the RAVDESS corpus (Livingstone & Russo, 2018). Actors say the same sentence, “Kids are talking by the door”, either calm or angry, at normal or strong intensity, twice. The repository includes the 32 clips of actors 01–04; the precomputed features for all 192 clips (24 actors) are in data/ravdess_features.csv.
RAVDESS encodes the design in the filename, e.g. 03-01-05-01-01-01-12.wav:



Position
Field
Codes




3
Emotion

4

01 = normal, 02 = strong


6

01, 02


7

01–24 (odd = male, even = female)




emo_dir   <- file.path(data_dir, "3_ravdess")
emo_files <- list.files(emo_dir, pattern = "\\.wav$")

parts <- str_split(str_remove(emo_files, "\\.wav$"), "-", simplify = TRUE)
meta <- tibble(
  file      = emo_files,
  emotion   = if_else(parts[, 3] == "02", "Calm", "Angry"),
  intensity = if_else(parts[, 4] == "01", "Normal", "Strong"),
  actor     = as.integer(parts[, 7]),
  sex       = if_else(actor %% 2 == 0, "Female", "Male")
)

title: Hands-on Lab: Does Anger Sound Different from Calm?
text:
A first look: actor 01

ex_calm  <- readWave(file.path(emo_dir, "03-01-02-01-01-01-01.wav"))
ex_angry <- readWave(file.path(emo_dir, "03-01-05-01-01-01-01.wav"))
# listen(ex_calm); listen(ex_angry)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
oscillo(ex_calm,  colwave = "#115C2E", title = "Calm")
oscillo(ex_angry, colwave = "#6A1F6E", title = "Angry")








Careful: oscillo() and spectro(dB = "max0") scale each clip to its own maximum, so side-by-side plots hide the loudness difference. bind() puts both clips on one shared scale:

spectro(bind(ex_calm, ex_angry), flim = c(0, 4), osc = TRUE, dB = "max0")














Exercise 1 · Listen & look (8 minutes, pairs)




Pick another actor (02, 03 or 04). Plot their calm vs. angry clip side by side, then on one shared scale with bind().
Which cue gives anger away first: amplitude, duration, or where the energy sits in frequency?
Run timer() with threshold = 5 and threshold = 10 on the calm clip. Which onset matches what you hear?

Deliverable: one sentence naming the cue, plus the threshold you would use.



# YOUR TURN ---------------------------------------------------------------
# my_actor <- "02"
# calm  <- readWave(file.path(emo_dir, paste0("03-01-02-01-01-01-", my_actor, ".wav")))
# angry <- ...







Solution: Exercise 1






my_actor <- "02"
calm  <- readWave(file.path(emo_dir, paste0("03-01-02-01-01-01-", my_actor, ".wav")))
angry <- readWave(file.path(emo_dir, paste0("03-01-05-01-01-01-", my_actor, ".wav")))

spectro(bind(calm, angry), flim = c(0, 4), osc = TRUE, dB = "max0")







on5  <- timer(calm, threshold = 5,  plot = FALSE)$s.start[1]
on10 <- timer(calm, threshold = 10, plot = FALSE)$s.start[1]
c(threshold_5 = on5, threshold_10 = on10)

 threshold_5 threshold_10 
    1.006672     1.116839 


The angry clip has much larger amplitude excursions and more energy above 1 kHz. A low threshold can lock onto low-level noise before speech starts; always check the onset against what you hear.

title: Hands-on Lab: Does Anger Sound Different from Calm?
text:
Hear the microphone
Same speaker, same text, seven devices (from Busquet, Efthymiou & Hildebrand 2024). First the average spectrum of each device. Note that meanspec() rescales every panel to its own maximum, so differences in level are hidden.

mic_dir   <- file.path(data_dir, "2_micTests")
mic_files <- list.files(mic_dir, pattern = "^[0-9]_audio.*\\.wav$")

par(mfrow = c(3, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (f in mic_files) {
  w <- readWave(file.path(mic_dir, f))
  if (w@stereo) w <- mono(w, "left")
  meanspec(w, flim = c(0, 10), main = str_remove(f, "\\.wav$"), col = "#115C2E")
}








The spectrograms below put all seven devices on one shared scale: the same time axis (0–12 s), the same frequency range (0–10 kHz) and the same colour scale in dB relative to the loudest device. Now you can see both how loud each device records and where it rolls off the high frequencies.

spec_db <- function(w, wl = 1024) {
  sp <- seewave::spectro(w, wl = wl, ovlp = 50, plot = FALSE, norm = FALSE, dB = NULL)
  list(time = sp$time, freq = sp$freq, amp = sp$amp)   # linear amplitude, not normalised
}
mic_specs <- map(set_names(mic_files, str_remove(mic_files, "\\.wav$")), function(f) {
  w <- readWave(file.path(mic_dir, f))
  if (w@stereo) w <- mono(w, "left")
  spec_db(w)
})

ref_max <- max(map_dbl(mic_specs, ~ max(.x$amp)))   # one reference for all devices
db_floor <- -80
t_max <- 12      # seconds, longest recording
f_max <- 10      # kHz
cols <- colorRampPalette(c("white", "#EAF4EE", "#249662", "#115C2E", "#3B1440"))(64)

par(mfrow = c(4, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4, 2, 1), mgp = c(2.3, 0.7, 0))
for (nm in names(mic_specs)) {
  sp <- mic_specs[[nm]]
  db <- pmax(20 * log10(sp$amp / ref_max + 1e-12), db_floor)
  keep <- sp$freq <= f_max
  image(sp$time, sp$freq[keep], t(db[keep, ]), col = cols, zlim = c(db_floor, 0),
        xlim = c(0, t_max), ylim = c(0, f_max), useRaster = TRUE,
        xlab = "Time (s)", ylab = "Frequency (kHz)", main = nm)
}
# shared colour legend
plot.new(); plot.window(xlim = c(db_floor, 0), ylim = c(0, 1))
rect(seq(db_floor, 0, length.out = 65)[-65], 0.35, seq(db_floor, 0, length.out = 65)[-1], 0.65,
     col = cols, border = NA)
axis(1, at = seq(db_floor, 0, 20)); title(main = "dB relative to the loudest device", font.main = 1)

title: Hands-on Lab: Does Anger Sound Different from Calm?
text:
Acoustic features vs. voice embeddings
data/ravdess_embeddings.csv holds a 768-dimensional embedding per clip from a pre-trained speech model (via talk::talkEmbed() in the full course). Does the black box beat the named features?

emb <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "ravdess_embeddings.csv"))
dat <- rav %>% left_join(emb, by = "file")
emb_cols <- grep("^Dim", names(dat), value = TRUE)

run_lasso <- function(cols) {
  Xm <- as.matrix(dat[, cols]); set.seed(515)
  f  <- cv.glmnet(Xm[tr, ], y[tr], family = "binomial", alpha = 1)
  p  <- as.numeric(predict(f, Xm[te, ], s = "lambda.min", type = "response"))
  round(as.numeric(auc(roc(y[te], p, quiet = TRUE))), 3)
}
tibble(representation = c("Acoustic features", "Embeddings", "Both"),
       test_AUC = c(run_lasso(feat_cols), run_lasso(emb_cols), run_lasso(c(feat_cols, emb_cols))))

title: Mini exercises
text: Four short exercises carry you from listening to a research design. Exercises 1–3 run in the lab notebook, where each has a prepared YOUR TURN chunk and a folded solution. Exercise 4 needs only a pen.

title: Mini exercises
text:
Warm-up · Audacity (10′, demo)

10 minutes · follow along or watch

Open & compare: drag data/1_alexa/alexa_cmd1.wav and alexa_cmd2.wav into one project. Compare length, pauses and peaks.
Spectrogram view: track menu (the track name) → Spectrogram. Watch the harmonics rise in the frustrated command.
Plot a spectrum: select one vowel → Analyze → Plot Spectrum. Find F0 and the formants.
Edit, then re-check: Truncate Silence, and change pitch by ±2 semitones. What changes in what you hear, and in the picture?
Hear the microphone: load all files in data/2_micTests/. Same speaker, seven devices: which ones roll off the highs?

title: Mini exercises
text:
Exercise 1 · Listen & look

8 minutes · pairs · notebook block 2

Pick an actor (02, 03 or 04). Plot calm vs. angry oscillograms and spectrograms side by side.
Now bind() the two clips and plot them on one shared scale. What appears that was hidden?
Run timer() with threshold 5 and 10. Which onset matches what you hear?

Deliverable · One sentence naming the cue that gives anger away first, and the onset threshold you would use.

title: Mini exercises
text:
Exercise 2 · Feature extraction

12 minutes · individual → pairs · notebook block 4

Run voiceR::autoExtract() on the 32 trimmed clips.
Plot pitch_mean, pitch_sd, loudness_mean and HNR_mean by emotion, then add one spectral and one temporal feature of your choice.
Compare with the emotion-signature table from the slides, and check whether the effect holds for every actor.

Deliverable · The feature family that separates calm from angry best, and one feature that surprised you.




Emotion signatures from the slides: what theory predicts for each state.

title: Mini exercises
text:
Exercise 3 · Prediction

10 minutes · pairs · notebook block 5

Fit a lasso on all 192 clips, holding out whole actors. Re-run with a different seed: how stable is the AUC?
Compute AUC for female vs. male and for normal vs. strong intensity.
Name the first thing that would break if you used this model on customer-service calls.

Deliverable · Your AUC, the weakest subgroup, and one validity threat for field use.

title: Mini exercises
text:
Exercise 4 · Idea sprint

15 minutes · pairs → room

Pick one project of yours. Where could voice be the IV (manipulate a vocal cue), the DV (measure the voice) or the mediator?
Name the construct, the feature family that should move, and in which direction.
Name your data source (lab, online, field, voice agent) and the biggest validity threat.

Deliverable · A one-sentence pitch: “We will measure ___ in voice to show ___.” Two or three pairs share.

3 · Install the R packages
Open the downloaded folder in RStudio (double-click any file, or File → Open Project in New Session and choose the folder), set the working directory to the folder, and run:
source("setup/install_packages.R")
This installs tuneR, seewave, soundgen, tidyverse, glmnet, pROC and voiceR, and plays a quick test.






voiceR is currently installed from the CRAN archive



voiceR was archived on CRAN in June 2026, so install.packages("voiceR") fails. The setup script installs its dependencies and then the archived source package:
install.packages("https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/voiceR/voiceR_0.1.0.tar.gz",
                 repos = NULL, type = "source")
If that still fails on your machine, don’t worry: the notebook automatically falls back to soundgen::analyze(), the same feature engine voiceR uses.

text:

Open lab/voice_lab.qmd in RStudio and run the first two chunks (Setup and Warm-up). If you see two waveforms, you’re ready.

Run tuneR::setWavPlayer("/usr/bin/afplay") once, then listen() works.

title: Speech Analytics Bootcamp
text:
About the workshop
The human voice carries what surveys and clicks miss: emotion in real time, arousal and stress, confidence, and spontaneous reactions before conscious reflection. Smart speakers, voice assistants and LLM-based voice agents now make voice data cheap to collect at scale, yet most behavioural researchers lack the tools to use it.
This condensed workshop introduces voice as a behavioural data layer. We cover how speech is produced, which acoustic features map onto which psychological states, and where construct validity breaks down. In the hands-on lab you work with real emotional speech (calm vs. angry speakers): you listen in Audacity, plot waveforms and spectrograms in R, extract acoustic features with voiceR, and test whether those features separate the two states. We close with voice-based conversational agents for data collection, the ethics of voice data, and a short sprint on your own research ideas. No prior voice analytics experience is needed.



Same words, different meaning: two commands from a frustrated Alexa user.

title: Speech Analytics Bootcamp
text:
Learning outcomes

 01Argue for voiceExplain why voice is a distinct behavioural data source and where it adds value over text and self-report.
 02Map features to constructsLink pitch, loudness, spectral, voice-quality and timing features to psychological states, and name the main validity threats.
 03Run a minimal pipelineLoad audio, plot waveforms and spectrograms, trim, extract features and compare conditions in R.
 04Design with voiceSketch how voice enters your own studies as IV, DV or mediator, including via voice agents.
